1 Introduction to Statistics

1.1 High-Profile Applications of Statistics

  • •

    Statistics is a huge subject and it enjoys a critical role in a large variety of important disciplines. Some high-profile applications of Statistics include:

    • –

      Galaxy Formation (see movie)

    • –

      Climate Science (see movie)

    • –

      Covid Modelling

    • –

      Medical Science

    • –

      Pharmaceutical Industry

    • –

      Physics (discovery of the Higgs Boson, gravitational wave detection, etc.)

    • –

      Biological sciences (genetics, systems biology, etc.)

    • –

      Military Defence

    • –

      Computer Sciences/Machine Learning/AI

    • –

      Data Science (obviously!)

    • –

      Banking/finance

    • –

      Economics/econometrics

    • –

      Geology/oil industry

    • –

      Government analysis (at most levels)

  • •

    While the above areas may each seem very different, they share similar structures and similar problems that Statistics is well placed to solve.

  • •

    E.g. practitioners in these areas may

    • (a)

      utilise a mathematical model to represent key quantities of interest in the real world,

    • (b)

      have knowledge and observed data that relates imperfectly to limited aspects of the real world and of the model,

    • (c)

      want to understand features and behaviours of the real world,

    • (d)

      want to predict future behaviour.

  • •

    In short, Statistics facilitates all of this. Without appropriate use of Statistics, an analysis may be fundamentally limited or even utterly flawed.

1.2 What is Statistics?

  • •

    So, what actually is Statistics? I have asked this question of first year Undergraduates (who have notably studied Statistics previously at school) several times, and received the following interesting but incomplete answers:

    • –

      “It is a set of tools to help us analyse data”: No, data analysis is a useful part of Statistics but by no means the whole.

    • –

      “It is applied probability”: No, we certainly do apply probability within Statistics, but again this is a tool we use, and does not define the subject.

    • –

      “It is the study of informative summaries of data and their behaviour”: This is getting better, and is close to an old fashioned definition (where the word “Statistics” actually comes from), but is now again only a subset of the full subject.

  • •

    So what the hell is it then?

A possible definition of Statistics

  • •

    Perhaps a more general definition of Statistics is much more concise:

    • –

      It is the (mathematical) study of uncertainty.

  • •

    Or in slightly more detail:

    • –

      Statistics involves the mathematical representation of key real world quantities of interest and their associated uncertainties (often, but not always, using probability), the coherent incorporation of any (uncertain) knowledge, information or observed data into this framework, and the subsequent learning/inference, prediction, future experimental design and decision making in the presence of uncertainty that this structure facilitates.

  • •

    Quite the mouthful!

1.3 Full-scale War: Frequentists Vs. Bayesians

  • •

    So this all seems fine, but there is a problem.

  • •

    There is a major war going on within Statistics, based around two fundamentally opposed schools of thought:

    • –

      Frequentist Statistics: traditional, more established, simple to apply in certain cases (what you saw at school), but with questionable interpretation.

    • –

      Bayesian Statistics: modern/upcoming, more elegant, more powerful, but often more complex and requires more input.

  • •

    How can this be, that we have two competing approaches? Surely one of them is just “right”?

  • •

    The division can be understood as coming from fundamental differences in how one views probability:

    • –

      The Relative Frequency interpretation of probability underpins Frequentist Statistics.

    • –

      The Subjective (or personal, or betting) interpretation of probability underpins Bayesian Statistics.

  • •

    This is an unusual situation where a seemingly subtle philosophical difference would lead you to a different statistical paradigm, which in turn would lead you to make different decisions about real world problems (and which has sadly led in some cases to demonstrably poor decision making, resulting ultimately in many human deaths).

  • •

    Standard Maths or Stats degrees would often teach you the traditional Frequentist Statistics first, and leave Bayesian statistics for later years in the degree.

  • •

    We (our Statistics group) have recently taken the more modern view that you should be taught both sides of the controversy. Hence this course will introduce you to both Frequentist and Bayesian paradigms in the first year.

Motivating Example 1: Covid-19 Disease Test

  • •

    A new test for Covid-19 has been developed.

  • •

    It is fast and cheap, but has moderate accuracy.

  • •

    It has been tested on a limited set of people with known Covid status.

  • •

    You are selected at random from the UK population in August 2020 and you test positive, what is the probability that you have Covid-19?

  • •

    If instead you were selected at random from the London population in Jan 2021, what is the probability then?

We will examine this in a Bayesian framework, using some techniques you learned in the Probability course. Then we will extend and examine them further.

Motivating example 2: US Presidential Election Polling Pennsylvania State.

  • •

    It is the 22nd Oct 2024, two weeks before the 2024 US presidential election.

  • •

    You run a major polling company and you have conducted a large poll of people likely to vote across Pennsylvania State: a critical swing state in the election.

  • •

    Out of 1000 randomly chosen people 485 said they would vote for Harris, 515 for Trump (we will ignore “don’t knows/Libertarian party/Green Party” for now).

  • •

    Everyone wants to know your prediction: Multiple News networks keep calling (CNN, FOX etc), powerful Hedge funds are calling wanting an edge, calls from large military corporations are coming in too…

  • •

    What do you say about the possible result of the election? Do you trust what you would say, would you bet on it?

  • •

    We will analyse this in a Frequentist way (at first).

Brainstorm: Events, Randomness and Uncertainty

An event, A, is a statement (typically about the world) that may or may not be true. What is the difference between an event being random or an event being uncertain? With this in mind, which of these events are random and which are uncertain?

  • •

    the ground is wet,

  • •

    it will rain tomorrow,

  • •

    this dice roll will be a four,

  • •

    the average global climate temperature will increase by at least 2∘⁢C by 2050.

Overview

  • •

    Statistics is incredibly useful in many places where we want to make inferences or conclusions about the real world, and where there is some level of uncertainty. This course will teach you about the current war: Frequentists vs. Bayesians.

  • •

    We will play with the above two examples to give you a taste of what is possible, before subsequently going deeper into the Frequentist view first, followed by the Bayesian view. You can then choose your side…

1.4 Foundations of Statistics and the Interpretation of Probability

Here we recap some key properties of Probability, and discuss the all important interpretations of probability that underlie the different approaches to statistics.

1.4.1 Probability: Revision

Definition: Axioms of Probability (Revision)

For a sample space Ω representing the set of all possible outcomes of a scenario (or experiment or random phenomenon), with collection ℱ of events (each event may be viewed as a subset of the outcomes), the probability of event A, denoted P⁢(A), satisfies the axioms:

  • A1

    P⁢(A)≥0, for every A∈ℱ;

  • A2

    P⁢(Ω)=1; and

  • A3

    for A and B disjoint (i.e. A∩B=∅) then:

    P⁢(A∪B)=P⁢(A)+P⁢(B)

There is also a forth axiom A4 which provides the technical attribute of countable additivity, but we shall not focus on this here.

  • •

    The axioms of probability lead directly to the familiar attributes of probability, some basic ones being:

    • –

      0≤P⁢(A)≤1, so that all probabilities are expressed on the scale [0,1].

    • –

      P⁢(Ac)=1−P⁢(A), i.e. how to find the probability of the complement
      event ‘not A’.

    • –

      P⁢(Ω)=1 and P⁢(∅)=0, i.e. the sum of the probabilities for all/no possible outcomes is one/zero.

    • –

      various rules for combining probabilities (see more below).

Discussion: Issues with Probability and the Real World

Even the (hopefully familiar) axioms of probability raise some issues when we want to use probability in the real world:

  • •

    As we have that 0≤P⁢(A)≤1, where P⁢(A)=0 is viewed as representing that the outcome is impossible, and P⁢(A)=1 that the outcome is certain, we see that probability generalises the area of pure Logic, where we would typically have that a statement A was either TRUE =1 or FALSE =0.

  • •

    Values of P⁢(A) in between 0 and 1 could indicate our degree of belief in the likelihood of the event occurring, the higher the probability, the more likely we think the event: but what exactly is P⁢(A)? How do we choose its value?

  • •

    Also, when we speak of a scenario or experiment or random phenomenon for which the outcomes are unknown, what exactly do we mean? Something that we can repeat again and again? Each repetition of the experiment may be similar, but the initial conditions definitely won’t be identical. What if we cannot repeat it at all? This links to the important distinction between random and uncertain discussed above (Section 1.3).

  • •

    We see that the axioms of probability give a very useful framework for how our probabilities should behave (and if we use probabilities that break these rules we will rapidly get into trouble), but we also see that the axioms say nothing about how we should choose initial probabilities.

  • •

    This is analogous to a Logic proof (e.g. If C is TRUE and C⇒D then D is TRUE) not being able to tell you whether an initial premise is actually true in the real world (e.g. Question: so is C actually TRUE then? Logic answer is “absolutely no idea”).

  • •

    We see that to actually assign initial probabilities (i.e. choose their values) we need an interpretation of what probability means in the real world.

1.4.2 Interpretations of Probability.

  • •

    Most people have an intuitive feel for probability, and the Axioms seem to capture this quite well.

  • •

    However, if we want probability to make statements about the real world, then we must have a physical interpretation of the mathematics to help us assign initial probabilities. Without any interpretation, we are bound to get a little stuck!

  • •

    The Interpretation of Probability is highly controversial, with the most popular interpretations being the Classical, the Frequentist and the Subjective.

  • •

    Classical

    • –

      Based on the assumption of underlying equally likely events: e.g. the roll of a dice: each of the 6 sides is equally likely, therefore the probability of each side = 1/6.

    • –

      Not so good in more complex situations, e.g. what is the probability of the radioactive decay of a Ceasium atom in a certain time period?

    • –

      Also, rather pedantically, we could say that we never, ever, actually have a perfectly fair dice or coin etc.

  • •

    Frequentist

    • –

      More common interpretation based on relative frequencies for a repeatable experiment.

    • –

      An event A has probability P⁢(A) given by:

      P⁢(A)=limn→∞nAn,

      where nA is the number of times event A occurred in n (random?) repetitions of the experiment.

    • –

      Very intuitive, and how most people actually think about probability.

    • –

      Problems: does such a limit exist in our world? What does repeatable actually mean: what are the initial conditions each time (surely not the same)? More importantly, what about unrepeatable experiments? For example, what is the probability that it rains here tomorrow? What is the probability of a 3 degree increase in the mean global temperature by 2050?

    • –

      Underlies Frequentist Statistics.

  • •

    Subjective

    • –

      More controversial, where probabilities are viewed as personal (or subjective) beliefs about the likelihood of an event A occurring.

    • –

      Basic definition is that ‘Your’ probability for event A is the number p that you consider p pounds (£⁢p) a fair price to pay to take a gamble which will pay you £⁢1 if event A occurs and £⁢0 otherwise. Note that if you regard £⁢p a fair price, then you would have no preference between this bet, and the bet with price £⁢(1−p) which pays £⁢0 if event A occurs and £⁢1 otherwise.

    • –

      Can be defined in a precise way, and the Probability Axioms are actually derived as requirements of coherence (i.e. not being daft).

    • –

      Can subsume the two previous definitions (as these can be viewed as reasonable judgements) but can be extended to many more situations. For example, what is the probability of catastrophic climate change?

    • –

      Formalised by the great subjectivist probabilist and Statistician Bruno De Finetti (1906 -1985). In his famous book “Theory of Probability” he writes in the middle of a page:

      PROBABILITY DOES NOT EXIST

      (The capitalisation is De Finetti’s). By this he is asserting that Probability is all in our heads and is not an inherent physical property of the real world.

    • –

      Doesn’t suffer the problems of the other interpretations, however probabilities are different for each person, and can be hard to specify. (Also, what about Quantum Mechanics? Much controversy here.)

    • –

      Underlies the Theory of Bayesian Statistics.

1.4.3 A Summary of Useful Probability Results

Combining Events

  • •

    The event that either A or B or both occur is A∪B (union).

  • •

    The event that both A and B occur together is A∩B (intersection).

  • •

    These probabilities are related via the rule

    P⁢(A∪B)=P⁢(A)+P⁢(B)−P⁢(A∩B).
  • •

    Events are disjoint (incompatible, mutually exclusive) if they cannot occur at the same time.

  • •

    The Addition law for disjoint events: If A and B are disjoint events, then P⁢(A∩B)=0 and so

    P⁢(A∪B)=P⁢(A)+P⁢(B).

Conditional Probability and Independence

  • •

    For any two events A, B, the notation P⁢(A|B) denotes the conditional probability that event A occurs, assuming that the event B has already occurred.

  • •

    Conditional probabilities are either obtained directly, or by using the conditional probability rule:

    P⁢(A|B)=P⁢(A∩B)P⁢(B),for⁢P⁢(B)>0.
  • •

    Rearranging this equation gives the (general) multiplication rule, useful in simplifying probabilities: for any two events A, B:

    P⁢(A∩B)=P⁢(A|B)⁢P⁢(B).
  • •

    Two events are said to be independent when the occurrence of one has no bearing on the occurrence of the other. In terms of probability, if A,B are independent then

    P⁢(A|B)=P⁢(A)

    as the knowledge that B occurred is irrelevant.

Partitions

  • •

    Suppose that n events E1,…,En are disjoint, and suppose that exactly one must happen. Such a collection of events is called a (sure) partition.

  • •

    Now we can write any other event A in combination with this event: in general,

    P⁢(A)=P⁢(A∩E1)+P⁢(A∩E2)+…+P⁢(A∩En),

    which simplifies to

    P⁢(A) = P⁢(A|E1)⁢P⁢(E1)+P⁢(A|E2)⁢P⁢(E2)+…+P⁢(A|En)⁢P⁢(En)
    = ∑i=1nP⁢(A|Ei)⁢P⁢(Ei)

    using the multiplication rule.

  • •

    Often, this is the most convenient way of getting at certain hard-to-think-about events: to associate them with a suitable partition, and then use conditional probability to simplify matters.

Bayes Theorem

  • •

    For any two events A,B, the multiplication rule gives the formula

    P⁢(A∩B)=P⁢(A|B)⁢P⁢(B).
  • •

    Another equivalent formula is obviously

    P⁢(A∩B)=P⁢(B|A)⁢P⁢(A).
  • •

    By equating these two formulae and rearranging, we obtain the formula known as Bayes theorem:

    P⁢(A|B)=P⁢(B|A)⁢P⁢(A)P⁢(B).
  • •

    It is useful mainly as a way of “inverting” probabilities. Often, the probability in the denominator must be calculated using the simplifying method shown in the last section; i.e. via a partition.

  • •

    Underlies the majority of Bayesian Statistics.
